name: Peuls (Guidiguis)
overview: In the majority in Guidiguis, where they live with the Toupouri, the Fulani speak Fulfulde, a language widespread from Senegal to Cameroon. Coming from Mali via Nigeria and Guinea, they are organised in a lamidate (lamido, kaigama, kofa) and have deeply shaped their culture on Islam; livestock rearing, trade and the sale of milk provide their living.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, integrated with the Toupouri; some Fulani speak Toupouri.
Fulfulde is spoken in the North and Adamawa (Ngaoundéré, Maroua, Banyo…), as far as Bertoua, and throughout West Africa.
Marriage remains mostly endogamous; anyone who marries a Fulani must embrace Islam.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Land conquered by the ancestors.
Having come from Mali via Nigeria and Guinea, they have kept no ties with these places.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship: the lamido governs with his dignitaries (kaigama, kofa) and his notables (serkedjo), who decide through discussion and consensus.
The Gao, descended from a single clan, are hunters and soldiers.
Children greet their parents; women and children do not stare the father in the eye; the woman sits or bows to greet men.
Religious differences have sometimes set the Fulani against their Toupouri and Moundang neighbours.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the young woman joins her husband's family.
The boy becomes a man at around 17-18; the girl at around 15-16.
Marriage between cousins is common; formerly, parents chose the wife, today it is the young man.
Steps: proposal or search for a girl, negotiations, tegal (engagement), marriage; bride price in kind and in money, with cola and goat.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship: only the mosque and the prayer ground (sallikere) are sacred places.
Birth is a gift from God; death, the return to God. The dead may appear in dreams.
Taboo: talking about sexuality. Forbidden: adultery. In the past, adultery, murder and blasphemy were severely punished; today, human rights prevail.
No oracles, but great marabouts; cowries, water and a mirror are used for divination.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: livestock rearing, trade, farming. Women: selling milk, petty trade.
The land belongs to the men, by inheritance or acquisition.
Ancestral crafts: mats for sleeping and praying, caps against the heat, clay pots for storing water.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Boubou (saro), gandoura; wrapper and veil for women.
Traditional medicine is increasingly abandoned in favour of the hospital.
Beauty: the man of medium height, with a brown complexion, well-groomed and elegant; the woman with a beautiful face, a smile and a brown complexion.
Courtship: glances, gifts, dance steps; facial care and a smile in the woman.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Instruments: tam-tam (mbakgou), garaya (small traditional guitar).
Festivals: religious only, Tabaski and Ramadan.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The culture of the Fulani of Guidiguis has been largely shaped by Islam and the Arab world: names, festivals, beliefs and clothing bear its mark.

sections.title: The names
items: The name is given at the indéré, seven days after birth: an ox is slaughtered and people dance.
On converting to Islam, one takes a Koranic name, in addition to the family name.
Names are readily shortened: Abdoulaye becomes Abdou, Aïssatou Aïssa, Boubakari Bouba.

lessons.title: Who are the Peuls (Guidiguis)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Peuls (Guidiguis) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Peuls (Guidiguis) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Peuls (Guidiguis) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Peuls (Guidiguis) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Peuls (Guidiguis) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Peuls (Guidiguis) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, integrated with the Toupouri; some Fulani speak Toupouri. • Fulfulde is spoken in the North and Adamawa (Ngaoundéré, Maroua, Banyo…), as far as Bertoua, and throughout West Africa. • Marriage remains mostly endogamous; anyone who marries a Fulani man or woman must embrace Islam. • Land conquered by the ancestors. • Having come from Mali through Nigeria and Guinea, they have kept no ties with these places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in Guidiguis, where they live with the Toupouri, the Fulani speak Fulfulde, a language widespread from Senegal to Cameroon. Coming from Mali via Nigeria and Guinea, they are organised in a lamidate (lamido, kaigama, kofa) and have deeply shaped their culture on Islam; livestock rearing, trade and the sale of milk provide their living.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Peuls (Guidiguis) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Peuls (Guidiguis)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Peuls (Guidiguis), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Peuls (Guidiguis).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Peuls (Guidiguis), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Peuls (Guidiguis).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: maize couscous, porridge, sticky sauce (okra). • Drinks: milk, porridge. • Men: livestock rearing, trade, farming. Women: selling milk, small-scale trade.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Peuls (Guidiguis) eat mainly maize couscous, porridge, sticky sauce. Traditional drinks: milk, porridge. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Peuls (Guidiguis): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

student.memo: Among the Peuls (Guidiguis), dances accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, garaya. Festival(s): Tabaski, Ramadan.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Peuls (Guidiguis)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Peuls (Guidiguis), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Peuls (Guidiguis). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Peuls (Guidiguis), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Peuls (Guidiguis). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: livestock, trade, farming. Women: selling milk, petty trade. • Land belongs to men, by inheritance or acquisition. • Ancestral crafts: mats for sleeping and praying, caps against the heat, canaris for storing water.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: livestock rearing, trade, farming. Women: selling milk, petty trade. Land belongs to men, by inheritance or acquisition.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Peuls (Guidiguis)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Peuls (Guidiguis)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Peuls (Guidiguis), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Peuls (Guidiguis). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Peuls (Guidiguis), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Peuls (Guidiguis). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No ancestor worship: only the mosque and the prayer ground (sallikere) are sacred places. • Birth is a gift from God; death, the return to God. The dead may appear in dreams. • Taboo: talking about sexuality. Forbidden: adultery. In the past, adultery, murder and blasphemy were severely punished; today, human rights prevail. • No oracles, but great marabouts; cowries, water and a mirror are used for divination.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor worship: only the mosque and the prayer ground (sallikere) are sacred places. Birth is a gift from God; death, the return to God. The dead may manifest themselves in dreams.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Peuls (Guidiguis) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Fulfulde
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.langText: Mi hofni/ Sannou/ Alah hokedjam ,Allah honane/ mi sani

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Peuls (Guidiguis) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Peuls (Guidiguis) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Peuls (Guidiguis) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Peuls (Guidiguis) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Fulfulde. • Greeting formulae: Mi hofni/ Sannou/ Alah hokedjam ,Allah honane/ mi sani = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); A weeti djam na ? = morning greeting (one person); On weeti djam na ? = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Gootel, Didi, Tati, Nay, Djoy. • Names are readily shortened: Abdoulaye becomes Abdou, Aïssatou Aïssa, Boubakari Bouba. • The culture of the Fulani of Guidiguis has been largely shaped by Islam and the Arab world: names, festivals, beliefs and clothing bear its mark.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Fulfulde are the first steps towards communicating with the Peuls (Guidiguis). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Fulfulde.
